Why Higher Prices Mean Buying Less — Except When They Don't

When a price rises, the response splits in two: a substitution effect SESESE away from the pricier good, and an income effect IEIEIE from being effectively poorer. Usually they point the same way — but for an inferior good like instant noodles the income effect pushes back, and for a survival staple like rice it can win outright: the Giffen case, where a higher price means buying more.

Δx1=SE+IE\Delta x_1 = SE + IEΔx1​=SE+IE
IE>∣SE∣⇒GiffenIE > |SE| \Rightarrow \text{Giffen}IE>∣SE∣⇒Giffen

Examples & Exercises

A consumer with a lunch budget of 404040 and food 2 fixed at 888 sees food 1 rise from 444 to 666. How much does food 1 fall, and how does the drop split between the substitution and income effects?

Show proof
  1. The old bundle AAA splits the budget in half: food 1 555, food 2 2.52.52.5. At the new price, bundle CCC has food 1 down to 4012≈3.33\frac{40}{12} \approx 3.331240​≈3.33. The total effect is −1.67-1.67−1.67.
  2. To isolate substitution, top up the budget so the old basket stays affordable at new prices: 6×5+8×2.5=506 \times 5 + 8 \times 2.5 = 506×5+8×2.5=50. With 505050, bundle BBB picks food 1 5012≈4.17\frac{50}{12} \approx 4.171250​≈4.17 — the substitution effect is 4.17−5=−0.834.17 - 5 = -0.834.17−5=−0.83.
  3. The rest is the income effect: 3.33−4.17=−0.833.33 - 4.17 = -0.833.33−4.17=−0.83. For a consumer who likes both foods equally, the two effects split the drop exactly in half. Both negative is the signature of a normal good.

The price of rice rises from 444 to 555, yet one household starts buying more rice — 303030 up to 31.531.531.5. Is the law of demand broken?

Show proof
  1. This household must hit 707070 calories a day. Rice gives 222 calories per unit, meat 111; the budget is 240240240 and meat costs 121212. Initially rice 303030 and meat 101010 hit the target exactly.
  2. Dearer rice makes the same calories cost more money — the household is effectively poorer. The only luxury to cut is meat, which falls from 101010 to 6.96.96.9.
  3. The calorie hole left by the meat must be plugged with rice. The substitution effect is nearly zero, −0.01-0.01−0.01 — survival calories have no substitute — while the income effect is +1.58+1.58+1.58. Net: +1.57+1.57+1.57. Pricier, yet bought more. That is a Giffen good.
  4. This is not the luxury-goods story of "pricier sells better". There, the high price itself creates status value and preferences move; Giffen is made not by taste but by poverty.
